title: Speak with Confidence
subtitle: 28-Day Articulation & Presence Practice
notice: Practise off duty in a safe place, without distracting watchkeepers or active work. Examples are fictional communication drills. Vessel procedures, required reporting and standard marine phrases take priority. Self-checks record practice, not professional competence.

days.title: The Three-Sentence Opener
principles: Open with purpose, then the current situation, then the next action or decision. Give the listener a map before detail.
For a handover, this opener starts the conversation; complete every item required by the vessel’s handover procedure afterwards.
days.do: Use one idea per sentence and identify who owns the next action.
days.avoid: Compressing a required handover into three sentences or listing defects without priorities.
days.scenario: You are opening an engine-room watch handover after a maintenance period.
days.weak: There was a lot going on earlier, and I’ll try to remember everything. Anyway, there’s something about the job upstairs…
days.strong: I’ll start with the outstanding work for this watch. The maintenance job remains incomplete and the responsible engineer has been informed. Let’s confirm its status and responsibilities, then complete the handover checklist.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose a fictional handover and write purpose, situation and next action as three short lines.
1:00–2:00 — Say the opener twice, leaving a brief pause between sentences.
2:00–3:00 — Repeat without reading, then name the checklist you would continue with.
checks: I gave purpose, situation and next action in three distinct sentences.
I identified a responsible person or a clear question about ownership.
I treated the opener as the start of a complete handover.

days.title: Kill “Sorry” from Every Ask
principles: Make routine requests with a clear need, reason and time. Courtesy does not require apologising for doing your job.
Keep genuine apologies when you caused a problem: acknowledge it, own your part and explain the correction.
days.do: Say “Please confirm…” or “I need…” with a specific reason.
days.avoid: Repeated apologies before a legitimate request, or removing accountability when an apology is warranted.
days.scenario: You need clarification of a work instruction before the job can proceed.
days.weak: Sorry, Chief, sorry to bother you. It’s probably obvious, but could I maybe ask about that instruction?
days.strong: Chief, please clarify which work instruction applies to this job. I need to confirm the scope before we proceed. Can we check it together now?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write three routine requests you often make onboard.
1:00–2:00 — Remove unnecessary apologies; add the need and reason. Say each request aloud.
2:00–3:00 — Practise one real accountability statement: “I made the error. I’m sorry. Here is the correction.”
checks: My routine request states what I need and why.
My tone stays courteous without repeated apologies.
I can still give a genuine apology when responsible.

days.title: Kill “I Think Maybe”
principles: Separate an observation from an interpretation: what you saw, what you suspect and what remains unknown.
State the basis and timing of a report. Clear uncertainty is more credible than invented certainty.
days.do: Identify the indication or record and state when it was checked.
days.avoid: Presenting an unconfirmed diagnosis as fact or hiding uncertainty behind vague language.
days.scenario: A senior engineer asks whether a recurring indication proves that a component has failed.
days.weak: I think maybe that part is bad again. It sort of looks like what happened before.
days.strong: The indication has recurred on the panel. I haven’t confirmed the cause. I’ll report the recorded observations to the responsible engineer and follow the approved checks.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose a fictional equipment observation and label three lines: observed, suspected and unknown.
1:00–2:00 — Record a 30-second report and listen for unsupported certainty.
2:00–3:00 — Repeat with the evidence first and the uncertainty stated once.
checks: I clearly separated observation and interpretation.
I stated what remains unconfirmed.
I gave a next step within my authority.

days.title: Kill “Does That Make Sense?”
principles: Check understanding with a specific response: ask the listener to explain the next step or repeat the critical detail.
Treat a mismatch as a reason to clarify, not an opportunity to embarrass someone. Required standard communication procedures take priority.
days.do: Ask “What will you do first?” or “Please confirm the agreed responsibility.”
days.avoid: Treating a nod or a generic “yes” as evidence of comprehension.
days.scenario: You have explained the division of responsibilities during a planned maintenance briefing.
days.weak: So, that all makes sense, right? Good, let’s just get on with it.
days.strong: Before we finish, please confirm your assigned task and who you will contact if the scope changes. I’ll check that it matches the plan. We’ll clarify any differences now.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write a fictional instruction containing one task and one reporting point.
1:00–2:00 — Say it aloud, then ask a specific confirmation question.
2:00–3:00 — Role-play an incorrect reply and correct the misunderstanding calmly.
checks: I asked for a specific confirmation rather than a general yes.
I compared the reply with the intended message.
I corrected a mismatch respectfully.

days.title: “Tell Me About Yourself” in One Line
principles: Use role, relevant experience and immediate contribution. Keep the introduction useful to the person in front of you.
Describe only qualifications and experience you actually have. One sentence is an opener, not your entire career history.
days.do: Prepare a short version tailored to sign-on or a professional meeting.
days.avoid: A life story, exaggerated expertise or an introduction based only on an employer’s name.
days.scenario: You meet the chief engineer during sign-on and are invited to introduce yourself.
days.weak: Well, I’ve been around ships for a while, and there are lots of things I’ve done, so I suppose you’ll get to know me.
days.strong: I’m JV, joining as an oiler with LNG experience, and I’m ready to learn this vessel’s routines and support the engine team.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Fill in: “I’m [name], a [role] with [relevant experience], here to [contribution].”
1:00–2:00 — Say three versions for a chief engineer, a training instructor and a new crewmate.
2:00–3:00 — Choose the most natural version and deliver it without rushing.
checks: My introduction fits in one clear sentence.
My experience claims are accurate.
I made my contribution relevant to the listener.

days.title: Problem. Solution. Ask.
principles: State the problem and its operational relevance, offer a proposal, then make a concrete request.
Present the proposal as something to assess; do not imply a workaround is approved before the responsible person decides.
days.do: Distinguish facts, proposed action and requested authority.
days.avoid: Reporting a problem without a request or presenting an unapproved change as a settled decision.
days.scenario: You are updating the second engineer about an unclear job allocation.
days.weak: Nobody seems to know what’s happening with the job, and I guess we’ll need to figure something out.
days.strong: The job allocation has two conflicting versions, so ownership is unclear. I propose we reconcile them against the current plan before work starts. Can you confirm the final assignment?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Pick a low-risk fictional coordination problem.
1:00–2:00 — Write one sentence each for problem, proposal and request.
2:00–4:00 — Deliver a 30-second update twice; remove background that does not change the decision.
checks: I described the problem and why it matters.
I clearly labelled my proposal.
I asked for a specific decision or confirmation.

days.title: Own the First 8 Seconds
principles: Begin with purpose and relevance rather than an apology or long preamble. Eight seconds is a practice target, not a safety rule.
Use an attentive posture and a short pause; respect the person leading the briefing.
days.do: Open with what the team needs to focus on and invite attention.
days.avoid: Competing for authority, talking over an active callout or rushing through required risk controls.
days.scenario: You have been asked to introduce the purpose of a pre-job briefing.
days.weak: Okay, um, I don’t want to take too long, but I guess we should maybe talk a little before starting.
days.strong: Before we begin, we need a shared understanding of the job and its limits. I’ll outline the scope, then we’ll confirm the required controls with the person in charge.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write an opening sentence for a fictional briefing.
1:00–2:00 — Practise it in roughly eight seconds without squeezing the words.
2:00–3:00 — Add a pause and one sentence explaining what happens next.
checks: My first sentence established the purpose.
I spoke at an understandable pace.
I respected the briefing leader and required process.

days.title: Stop Overexplaining
principles: Give the key fact and its consequence first, then let the listener request detail.
Keep necessary safety facts and uncertainties even when shortening the message. Concise does not mean incomplete.
days.do: Use headline, impact and next step, with supporting evidence ready.
days.avoid: A chronological story before the main issue or deleting details that affect safety.
days.scenario: The chief engineer asks why a planned task has not been completed.
days.weak: First we went to the store, then someone called, and after that there were a few messages, and we couldn’t really finish…
days.strong: The task is incomplete because the specified part is unavailable. The outstanding work is recorded and the responsible engineer has been informed. I need confirmation of the revised plan.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Record a one-minute account of a fictional delay.
1:00–2:00 — Identify the main fact, consequence and requested next step.
2:00–4:00 — Deliver a 25-second version; check that it still contains every decision-critical fact.
checks: The main issue came before the backstory.
I retained the facts needed for a decision.
I can provide the supporting detail when asked.

days.title: Cut Filler Words
principles: Replace some fillers with brief pauses. The goal is understandable speech, not a perfect accent or zero hesitation.
Prepare the first sentence and group the rest into short ideas.
days.do: Pause between ideas and restart a sentence calmly when needed.
days.avoid: Speeding up to hide hesitation or criticising your accent.
days.scenario: You explain the status of a routine inspection during a departmental update.
days.weak: Um, like, we’ve, ah, basically done most of the checks, and, um, there’s something still left.
days.strong: Most scheduled checks are complete. [Pause.] One item remains open. [Pause.] The responsible engineer is reviewing it.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Record a 30-second fictional update and count fillers without judging yourself.
1:00–2:00 — Rewrite the opening sentence and mark two places to pause.
2:00–3:00 — Record again; compare clarity and pace rather than chasing a zero count.
checks: I used a pause instead of filling every silence.
My second recording is easy to follow.
I kept a natural pace and respectful self-talk.

days.title: Speak Under Pressure
principles: Make the immediate communication task small: report what is known, what is unknown and who needs to act.
Practise away from live operations. During a real alarm, follow the vessel’s response and reporting procedures rather than a coaching exercise.
days.do: Use a steady short report and direct it to the responsible person.
days.avoid: Speculation, theatrical confidence or delaying an urgent callout to polish your wording.
days.scenario: In a cabin role-play, a colleague asks about a fictional unexpected machinery alarm.
days.weak: It’s probably nothing, I think. Maybe it’s the same thing as last time, so I’m not really sure what to say.
days.strong: The alarm is indicated, and the cause is not yet confirmed. I’m informing the responsible engineer under the response procedure. I’ll report the verified observations as they become available.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write three fictional prompt cards: alarm, unexpected question and changed plan.
1:00–3:00 — Draw each card and give a 20-second known/unknown/next-step response.
3:00–4:00 — Repeat the hardest response with a calmer pace.
checks: I gave verified information without guessing a diagnosis.
I identified the reporting route or responsible person.
I practised without interfering with a real watch or alarm.

days.title: The Interview Opener
principles: Connect your current role, a real example of responsibility and your readiness to develop.
Support confidence with evidence. Do not claim a certificate, competence or promotion you have not earned.
days.do: Lead with a relevant contribution and an honest development goal.
days.avoid: A memorised sales speech or a list of unsupported strengths.
days.scenario: A fleet interviewer opens a promotion discussion with “Why are you ready for the next step?”
days.weak: I’ve been waiting a long time, and I think I’m hardworking, so I hope you’ll consider me.
days.strong: In my current role, I’ve taken responsibility for accurate records and reliable handovers. I can describe a recent example and the feedback I received. I’d like to discuss the competencies I still need to demonstrate for promotion.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose one genuine responsibility and one specific example.
1:00–3:00 — Deliver a 40-second opener twice, keeping claims tied to evidence.
3:00–4:00 — Add a sentence acknowledging one development need.
checks: I used a real example rather than a general claim.
I connected it to the role I want.
I acknowledged development needs honestly.

days.title: Answering Hard Questions
principles: Use Bridge & Commit: acknowledge the exact question, separate what you know, then commit to a verification route.
A bridge connects to relevant evidence; it must not dodge the question. Give a realistic follow-up time you can meet.
days.do: Say “I don’t have that verified” and explain where you will check.
days.avoid: Bluffing a limit, inventing a regulation or promising a time you cannot deliver.
days.scenario: An inspector asks for a technical detail you cannot verify from memory.
days.weak: I think the number is around that value, but I’m sure it’s fine. Anyway, we normally do the job another way.
days.strong: I don’t have the verified value in front of me. The approved reference is available through the responsible officer. May I retrieve it and return with the exact section?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — List three difficult questions you might be asked, without inventing their answers.
1:00–3:00 — Practise a 20-second response to each using acknowledge, known and verification.
3:00–4:00 — Check whether each promised follow-up is realistic.
checks: I acknowledged the actual question.
I admitted the limit of my knowledge plainly.
I offered a credible verification route.

days.title: Value & Negotiation
principles: Describe contribution with verifiable examples, then state the opportunity you want to discuss.
Treat negotiation as a two-way conversation. Pay and contract terms require accurate documents and the appropriate company process.
days.do: Connect evidence, requested opportunity and a practical next step.
days.avoid: Unsupported savings claims, threats or promises that trade away safety or compliance.
days.scenario: You are discussing development opportunities before re-contracting.
days.weak: I do more than other people, so I should get something better next time. You know how much effort I put in.
days.strong: I’ve documented my additional responsibilities and completed training. I’d like to discuss whether they support a development assignment next contract. What evidence and decision process would you need?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write one contribution you can substantiate.
1:00–2:00 — State one request without comparing yourself with colleagues.
2:00–4:00 — Role-play a request, a clarifying question and a realistic next step.
checks: My contribution is supported by records or examples.
My request is specific and respectful.
I invited the other person’s criteria and process.

days.title: Presenting to Senior Leadership
principles: Begin with the decision required, followed by impact, evidence and options.
Match the detail to the audience while keeping important constraints visible.
days.do: Keep a short spoken brief and a separate evidence pack.
days.avoid: Reading every slide or hiding unresolved risks to make the proposal look easier.
days.scenario: A superintendent asks for a short briefing on a recurring documentation problem.
days.weak: I made a long presentation about everything that happened this month. I’ll start on the first slide and go through it all.
days.strong: I’m asking you to confirm ownership of the document-control correction. Conflicting versions are causing rework. I have two options and the supporting examples ready for review.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose a fictional issue and write the decision needed.
1:00–3:00 — Deliver a 60-second brief: decision, impact, evidence and options.
3:00–4:00 — Repeat in 30 seconds, retaining the key constraint.
checks: The requested decision appeared near the start.
I linked the issue to its consequence.
I kept the evidence available without reading it all aloud.

days.title: The Shipboard Pitch
principles: Propose one change with a clear benefit and a way to evaluate it.
Identify approval, compatibility and training needs before suggesting an operational trial.
days.do: Offer a small, authorised evaluation with a defined owner.
days.avoid: Claiming a tool is safe or suitable just because it is convenient.
days.scenario: You want the department to consider a better system for locating approved manuals.
days.weak: We should buy this app because it looks good, and everyone could probably use it straight away.
days.strong: We spend time locating the current manuals. I propose reviewing an indexed access tool against our document-control requirements. Can the responsible officer assess suitability and nominate someone to evaluate it?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write one workflow frustration and the evidence you have.
1:00–3:00 — Give a 45-second pitch covering benefit, evaluation and approval.
3:00–4:00 — Answer “What would make us reject this idea?” honestly.
checks: I proposed one change rather than several unrelated ideas.
I named an evaluation and approval route.
I could explain a limitation of my proposal.

days.title: Handling Interruptions
principles: Distinguish an urgent safety interruption from an ordinary discussion interruption. Safety information takes priority.
For an ordinary interruption, acknowledge it and request a short space to complete the key point.
days.do: Keep your voice steady and return to the issue, not the person.
days.avoid: Competing in volume or blocking an urgent warning to finish your speech.
days.scenario: During a defect discussion, a colleague interrupts with a non-urgent explanation of an earlier event.
days.weak: Can you stop interrupting me? I’m trying to speak, and you always do this.
days.strong: I’ll come to that background next. Let me finish the current status in one sentence, then I want your input. If you have an immediate safety concern, please raise it now.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Prepare a 20-second status statement.
1:00–3:00 — Ask a partner to interrupt once, or play a recorded interruption; practise acknowledging and returning.
3:00–4:00 — Repeat with an urgent warning and deliberately yield the floor.
checks: I kept the response about the discussion, not someone’s character.
I requested a brief, specific space to finish.
I gave urgent safety information priority.

days.title: Say No Without Softening
principles: State a safety boundary directly, give the reason and identify the approved next step.
Use the vessel’s stop-work and escalation arrangements. Firmness does not grant authority to improvise procedures.
days.do: Say what cannot proceed and what must be confirmed first.
days.avoid: A vague objection, personal accusation or an unauthorised workaround.
days.scenario: Someone asks you to start a job while a required authorisation is still unresolved.
days.weak: I’m not really comfortable, but if you think it’s okay, maybe we can just try.
days.strong: I cannot proceed while the required authorisation is unresolved. I’m raising this with the person in charge under our procedure. We need confirmation before the job can start.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write a fictional boundary without naming real confidential work.
1:00–3:00 — Say boundary, reason and escalation three times in a calm voice.
3:00–4:00 — Respond to “We’re in a hurry” without weakening the boundary.
checks: My boundary was clear and specific.
I gave a reason without attacking anyone.
I named the approved escalation or confirmation route.

days.title: Push Back Without Aggression
principles: Acknowledge the shared objective, identify the conflict and request an authorised decision.
Separate schedule pressure from the requirements that govern the work.
days.do: Use neutral facts and propose a review of the plan.
days.avoid: Sarcasm, accepting a shortcut to please someone or claiming an unapproved alternative is safe.
days.scenario: A planned departure creates pressure to complete an unresolved job quickly.
days.weak: That schedule is ridiculous. If you want it done, you can take the blame.
days.strong: I understand the departure target. The present plan leaves a required condition unresolved. We need the responsible officer to review the conflict and confirm an authorised plan.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Name a shared objective and a fictional unresolved condition.
1:00–3:00 — Practise a 30-second pushback using objective, conflict and decision.
3:00–4:00 — Remove any blame words and repeat with a level tone.
checks: I acknowledged the shared objective.
I explained the conflict using facts.
I requested an authorised decision without trading away the requirement.

days.title: Professional Rapport with Executives
principles: Be prepared, curious and concise. A useful question often creates more rapport than forced familiarity.
Respect confidentiality and keep operational assurances within what you can verify and are authorised to discuss.
days.do: Introduce your role and ask a relevant, open question.
days.avoid: Gossip, flattery or promising that every issue is resolved.
days.scenario: You meet a visiting superintendent before a departmental discussion.
days.weak: Everything is perfect here, sir. I’ve heard a lot about you, and I know all the things happening in the fleet.
days.strong: I’m JV from the engine team. I’ve prepared the items our department was asked to discuss. Which part would you like us to prioritise during your visit?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write an accurate introduction and two role-relevant questions.
1:00–3:00 — Role-play an introduction, a question and a short listening response.
3:00–4:00 — Identify one subject that should remain confidential.
checks: I introduced my role accurately.
I asked a relevant question and allowed time to answer.
I avoided unverified assurances and confidential details.

days.title: Maritime Networking Openers
principles: Start with a shared context, a specific question and a short introduction.
Build a conversation before asking for a favour, job referral or contact details.
days.do: Listen for a genuine connection and ask permission before following up.
days.avoid: A sales pitch, interrogation or adding someone to a group without consent.
days.scenario: You meet another engineer during a break at a shore-based training course.
days.weak: Hi, can you recommend me to your company? Give me your number and I’ll send you everything.
days.strong: That case study on handovers was useful. What part stood out to you? I’m JV, an engineer working on LNG vessels.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write two opening questions linked to a fictional seminar.
1:00–3:00 — Practise a 45-second conversation with more listening than self-description.
3:00–4:00 — Close with a permission-based follow-up request.
checks: My opener related to the shared setting.
I asked a question rather than immediately requesting a favour.
I asked permission for any follow-up.

days.title: Client & Auditor Conversations
principles: Answer the actual question with accurate information and the relevant record.
If you do not know or do not own the subject, say so and involve the responsible officer. Do not conceal deficiencies.
days.do: Make the evidence traceable and let the inspector complete the question.
days.avoid: Guessing, arguing, volunteering confidential information outside scope or coaching someone to hide a problem.
days.scenario: During an inspection, you are asked to show the current record for a task in your area.
days.weak: We always do it properly. I’m sure the record is somewhere, so there shouldn’t be a problem.
days.strong: This is the current record available to me. The responsible officer can confirm the outstanding entry. I’ll refer that part of your question to them rather than guess.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose a fictional record request and define what you know.
1:00–3:00 — Role-play a question, a concise answer and an evidence reference.
3:00–4:00 — Practise admitting one genuine limit without becoming defensive.
checks: I answered the question asked.
I distinguished the available record from an unverified claim.
I involved the responsible person when necessary.

days.title: The One-Sentence Status Update
principles: Combine current state, important exception and next step in one sentence.
Use this as a brief update only; required logs, handovers and emergency reports still need their full content.
days.do: Name the subject and the relevant time or context.
days.avoid: “All good” when an important exception remains open.
days.scenario: The chief engineer asks for a quick update on a planned document review.
days.weak: Yeah, mostly fine, we’re getting there, and there are a few bits still happening.
days.strong: The document review is complete except for one unresolved revision, which the responsible engineer is checking before final confirmation.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write three fictional status updates as state, exception and next step.
1:00–2:00 — Say each in one sentence without speaking faster.
2:00–3:00 — Ask whether any missing fact would change the listener’s decision.
checks: I named the subject and current state.
I included the important exception.
I identified the next step without replacing a required detailed report.

days.title: Speaking Up First
principles: Raise a relevant safety concern early, using observation and consequence rather than blame.
Do not wait for a polished presentation when an immediate warning is needed; use the vessel’s established communication and escalation procedures.
days.do: State the concern clearly and request attention or review.
days.avoid: Waiting for someone more senior to notice or turning a concern into a personal accusation.
days.scenario: At the start of a planning meeting, you notice that two versions of the job scope are being discussed.
days.weak: Maybe I’ll mention it later if someone asks. It’s probably not my place to say.
days.strong: Before we agree the plan, I need to flag a scope mismatch. These two versions assign different work. Can the person in charge confirm which one is current?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write a fictional concern using observation, consequence and request.
1:00–3:00 — Deliver it as your first contribution in a mock meeting.
3:00–4:00 — Practise repeating the concern respectfully if it is not acknowledged.
checks: I raised the relevant concern early.
I used an observable fact rather than blame.
I asked for a clear review or acknowledgement.

days.title: Reading the Room in 8 Seconds
principles: Use a brief scan to notice attention, noise and possible communication barriers. Eight seconds is a coaching cue, not a diagnostic test.
Confirm impressions with a question. Appearance alone cannot establish fatigue, comprehension or readiness for duty.
days.do: Check whether people can hear, understand and participate.
days.avoid: Assuming silence means agreement or diagnosing a colleague from body language.
days.scenario: You are about to begin a toolbox talk after a demanding shift change.
days.weak: Everyone looks fine. Nobody has complained, so I’ll go through this quickly.
days.strong: Before we begin, can everyone hear me and follow the briefing? If fatigue or another concern could affect participation, please raise it through our reporting process. We’ll confirm understanding as we go.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Imagine a briefing with noise, mixed language ability or low engagement.
1:00–2:00 — Pause, scan the imagined setting and name only observable conditions.
2:00–4:00 — Practise two respectful check-in questions and a specific comprehension check.
checks: I separated an observation from an assumption.
I asked a respectful check-in question.
I did not treat a quick scan as proof of fitness or comprehension.

days.title: Land a “Yes” in Three Sentences
principles: Make the need, evidence and requested decision easy to understand.
A sound request must also allow a reasoned no, a different option or further review. Clarity is not pressure to approve.
days.do: Specify the item, operational reason and decision owner.
days.avoid: Manufactured urgency, hiding alternatives or promising guaranteed results.
days.scenario: You are requesting review of a requisition for a missing specified tool.
days.weak: We really need more tools, and it would be great if you could approve something soon.
days.strong: The specified tool for the planned task is not available in our inventory. I’ve attached the requirement and the available alternatives for review. Can you confirm the requisition decision or advise what further information is needed?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Select a fictional requisition and identify its evidence.
1:00–3:00 — Give a three-sentence request, then answer one reasonable objection.
3:00–4:00 — Practise accepting a request for more information professionally.
checks: I stated a specific need and supporting evidence.
I asked for a decision from the appropriate person.
I allowed review rather than pressuring for automatic approval.

days.title: Handling “Send Me the Deck Offline”
principles: When asked to send material for later review, confirm what decision it supports, who owns it and when to follow up.
Keep urgent safety escalation separate from routine presentation follow-up. Sending slides is not approval to proceed.
days.do: Send a short summary with the evidence and an agreed follow-up.
days.avoid: Repeated vague reminders, assuming silence means approval or relying on an inbox for an immediate safety concern.
days.scenario: A superintendent ends your routine proposal discussion by asking you to send the slides later.
days.weak: Sure, I’ll send everything. I hope you can look at it sometime.
days.strong: I’ll send the brief and supporting evidence today. The decision needed is whether to authorise an evaluation, not immediate implementation. When would you prefer me to follow up, and is anyone else needed for review?
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write a subject line and one-sentence decision request for a fictional proposal.
1:00–3:00 — Practise a spoken close confirming recipient, decision and follow-up.
3:00–4:00 — Rewrite a vague reminder into a short, courteous follow-up.
checks: I clarified the requested decision and recipient.
I agreed or requested a follow-up time.
I did not confuse a sent document with authorisation.

days.title: Owning the Safety/Department Meeting
principles: Use an agenda with a purpose, decisions and action owners. Speak in short sections and invite concerns.
A stable stance, comfortable breathing and deliberate pauses can support delivery. Do not force your voice or judge confidence by accent.
days.do: Summarise decisions and verify who will do what next.
days.avoid: Dominating the room, reading every note or ending without action ownership.
days.scenario: You have been asked to chair a short departmental improvement meeting.
days.weak: We’ll just talk about whatever comes up. I have a lot to say, so I’ll go through my notes first.
days.strong: We have three items and two decisions to make. I’ll keep each discussion focused and invite concerns before we close it. At the end, we’ll confirm the actions, owners and follow-up dates.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Write an agenda containing three items and one decision.
1:00–3:00 — Deliver the opening while standing or sitting comfortably; pause between agenda items.
3:00–5:00 — Role-play the closing summary with named owners and agreed follow-up.
checks: I gave the meeting a clear purpose and structure.
I made space for concerns and other voices.
I closed with confirmed actions and owners.

days.title: The Final Pitch & Execution
principles: Combine purpose, evidence, honest uncertainty, options and a specific request in a coherent brief.
Judge success by understanding and an appropriate next step, not whether you always win agreement.
days.do: Rehearse, invite a challenge and follow through on commitments.
days.avoid: Overclaiming competence, hiding a limitation or treating completion of this course as professional certification.
days.scenario: You present a fictional improvement proposal to the chief engineer and superintendent.
days.weak: I’ve practised a lot, so I’m sure this will work. I just need everyone to agree, and we can figure out the details later.
days.strong: I’m proposing a reviewed change to how we locate approved documents. The examples show avoidable rework, but suitability still needs assessment. I’m asking for an evaluation owner and review date before any implementation decision.
drill: 0:00–1:00 — Choose one fictional proposal and identify the evidence, uncertainty and requested decision.
1:00–3:00 — Record a 90-second brief, then listen for structure, pace and unsupported claims.
3:00–5:00 — Answer one challenge and repeat a shorter version; compare it with your Day 1 recording if available.
checks: My brief connected purpose, evidence, uncertainty and request.
I handled a challenge without bluffing or becoming defensive.
I named a realistic follow-up and one skill to keep practising.
